It's a little more complicated than that.

All live service games launch largely half finished. The goal is a mechanism to net enough sales from a half finished game to give you real data on whether or not it will pay off to finish the game, or abandon it for another product. The model is supposed to help avoid risk because the assumption is as you "complete" the game your fans will convert new sales and you eventually will see the same total revenue as launching feature complete while being able to get to that point without as much upfront capitol.

It's like making a video-game on margin, with all the same fiscal pros and cons.

The trouble with the model is that if you aren't honest about it, you leave fans feeling burned and as you "finish" the game into what it was supposed to be may still be disinclined to advocate the product for new sales.

These "the division" and "destiny" service looter shooters usually appear in gaming news when they release patches for a reason; they pay for articles. They need people to become aware how far along they are to a feature complete product so they can capture each new segment of the demand curve that's willing to pay for the current level of "completeness", since games journalists are bigger whores than actual prostitutes it's easy to pay to make sure a patch is newsworthy.

The best ideas come from problems you already need to solve, but here are some thoughts:

That garage door motor is only meant to run for a few seconds at a time, it may have overheating issues if you try running it for longer periods. I found this one out with an old vacuum cleaner motor - especially if they're only cooled by ambient air, continuous runtime is asking a lot of these motors.

Take a look at the motor system. Is it brushed? Brushless? Are there any capacitors or diodes in line with the motor in the control box? These are things that can tell you more about its performance, etc. If there's a clamping diode in the control box you should definitely get something similar to go with the motor in its new location.
